utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Hannis, is there any -- Ms. Loukas, you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just in relation to Mr. Krajisnik's laptop, there appears to be some technical difficulty that the AV representative is attempting to fix and I just want to ensure that -- is there anything else that needs to be done? No, there's still a problem, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is the problem such that we could not proceed at this moment or is it something that could be fixed while we are ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There's apparently something wrong with the mouse, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. So I really can't offer an opinion in relation to its sustainability.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were a couple of procedural matters that I wanted to address before the witness came in. I don't know if it would be all right to do that while the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it we could start dealing with some procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour, I don't have a problem with that because I think the audio is obviously working; it's a problem with the laptop. So Mr. Krajisnik can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The first matter I wanted to bring to the Court's attention relates to the physical health condition of this witness. He has a number of ailments and he -- to my observation, during proofing, is in -- often times in a great deal of pain. I indicated to him that he should let Your Honours or me know if at any time he needed to take a break earlier than the normally scheduled one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll repeat that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Second, with regard to the witness's ICTY statement which we propose to offer through Rule 89(F), Ms. Loukas had advised me in the e-mail yesterday afternoon after I had left that there was one sentence she would like to have removed and I have no objection. I agree with that. I unfortunately had made copies and given those to the Court and everyone else before now, but for the record, I would indicate it is in paragraph 6 on page 2 of the English version of the statement. It's the next to the last sentence which reads, "It was obvious that they escaped in a helicopter." We agree that it is appropriate to remove that sentence and if we can strike it in the copy that's an exhibit or we'll make a substitute page, whichever works for the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then the interpreters are alarmed by the -- that there be a light change on that part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Finally with regard to this witness, in the proofing yesterday, I learned that he apparently has testified in Bosnia in two state prosecutions in Bosnia related to the war, once about five or six years ago and once last year, apparently regarding Batkovic camp where he was detained. This was a first that we -- that I became aware of it. We don't have those testimonies. I have advised Ms. Loukas of that. We will make the arrangements to try and track down whatever statement or testimony he might have given in connection with those cases, provide them to the Defence, and if it arises that there's something that should require him to return at a later date or if the parties can reach some kind of stipulation, if there's something that goes to credibility or what he testifies here, we would address it later but we would like to proceed with him today since he's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can indicate that Mr. Hannis e-mailed we yesterday in relation to this particular issue suggesting that particular course, and I think basically, in view of his -- whilst the normal procedure would be that it would be important to have all the relevant information here and now, I think in view of the fact that the witness is here, his apparent health issues, the Defence agrees with the course suggested by Mr. Hannis and we are content to proceed with the witness today and should an issue subsequently when this material comes up then we can come to some sort of an arrangement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will then follow the course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you counsel and Your Honour. The last matter I wanted to address, Your Honour, regarded scheduling. I anticipate that I will finish my direct of this witness in -- hopefully by the first break, the normally scheduled break at 10.30. And so I anticipate that we will be finished with him before the end of the day and ready to start with the second witness; however, I've spoken with Mr. Margetts who will be leading the next witness, KRAJ 671 Izmet Mehinagic who will testify openly without protective measures and there -- I know there are some matters regarding the documents related to him. There is a diary which apparently we only have a summary translation and Ms. Loukas has requested -- would like to have the full translation. Because those matters are still pending, if the Court is agreeable, we would like to propose that when we finish with this witness today, if it's early, we finish early and start with Mr. Mehinagic first thing in the morning. As Your Honours know, this is a week we only have two witnesses. We have had problems scheduling witnesses for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are aware of that. The Chamber is aware of that. I see that -- Mr. Krajisnik, is it true that the mouse problems have been solved or not? I do understand that someone tries to find a new mouse for you. You don't have a touch pad on that computer which would temporarily help you out? Because on my laptop I can choose but ... I don't know whether it's the touch pad or whether it's the mouse that's not functioning but.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither the touch pad nor the mouse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I wonder whether a new mouse would help you out. Mr. Krajisnik, could we start and then just temporarily you make some written notes and then we hope that the problem will be resolved soon or ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope so. I hope that it will be solved soon because I wouldn't like to disrupt the proceedings. I believe that the Trial Chamber should proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for your cooperation. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might briefly indicate while the witness is settling himself in that further technical assistance is required in relation to actually obtaining another computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- Ms. Loukas, we might need specific approval because not every computer is the same in terms of security regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I see, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuralic, first of all, good morning and apologies that we are discussing other matters when you came in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuralic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Kuralic. Mr. Kuralic, the Chamber has been informed about your health problems. Please do not hesitate to address the Chamber if you feel that it's difficult for you to continue. We'll then take a break and adapt our schedule to your abilities in terms of health. Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kuralic, what I would like to do is show you a copy of your ICTY statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May this be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit P642.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kuralic, that's your ICTY statement dated the 27th of June, 1996. Before coming to court today, did you have a chance to review that statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Today or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before today?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the course of reviewing that, did you note a few corrections that we discussed together?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, I want to show you a document, Mr. Kuralic, which lists some of the corrections and modifications that you agreed that should be made to your statement. You haven't seen this document yet, we were typing it up when we were proofing with you yesterday. If you can just take a moment to read that and let us know if we've listed the corrections that you suggested we make.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry I couldn't hear your answer from the translators. Does that contain the suggestions that you agreed we made to your statement after reviewing it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And attached to that supplemental information form is what appears to be a newspaper article. Can you tell us where that comes from, that article?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: This article was published by Kalesija municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, before we continue, could first Madam Registrar give a number to the supplemental information sheet and the attached -- would you like to have that two separate numbers or.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then the supplemental information sheet ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will be Prosecution Exhibit P643.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the newspaper article is attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kuralic, that's the newspaper in the municipality where you lived?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately -- I'm sorry. Do you recall approximately when that was published, when that story was put in the paper?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: After my release from the camp in 1993, I was released on the 10th of April and this article might have then been published in May or June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with those changes that we've listed in the supplemental information sheet, can you confirm to the Judges that your ICTY statement from 1996 as modified by that supplemental information and the newspaper article, is that a truthful and accurate account of your experiences during the war in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I haven't understood, I'm afraid. If you could repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Certainly, I'm sorry. Is that ICTY statement you gave when read together with the supplemental information, the corrections, and your newspaper article, when all those are read together, is that a truth and accurate account of what happened to you in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Of course it is accurate, but it is only a portion of what happened because a person cannot possibly relate everything that happened in the course of 325 days. It does take a lot more time than I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to tender those two exhibits, 642 and 643, pursuant to 89(F), and I would like to read in a summary at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the portion it seems you agreed to take out, would that have any consequence for the corresponding line in the statement? I do understand that it might relate at least from what I heard, that it might relate to -- or is it from the summary or from the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's from the statement, Your Honour and it's not mentioned in the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may then Your Honour, I'd like to -- Mr. Kuralic Mr. Kuralic, I'm going to read a summary of what's in your statement now and then I will have some questions for you. Mirsad Kuralic is a Bosnian Muslim metal worker from Kalesija municipality. In April 1992, he helped provide food and shelter to some of the 1.200 Muslim refugees fleeing from Zvornik municipality. He was drafted into the Bosnian army and from mid-April was at the front line around Kalesija. On 30 May 1992, while on an armed reconnaissance, the witness and three comrades encountered a larger group of Serb fighters. In the ensuing skirmish, a Serb officer and two of the witness's comrades were killed. The witness was captured. He was taken to the Serb command post in Memici where he was beaten, stabbed, cut on his face and leg, and burned with cigarettes. He was further brutalised during his subsequent transport to Vlasenica where he was interrogated. After his interrogation, he was left alone for three days in a small room with his hands handcuffed behind his back. He received no food, water, or medical attention. He was then placed in the sports hall with other POWs for about four days after which he was in a group of about 400 that were taken to Susica camp. After a brief stay there where he encountered camp manager Dragan Nikolic, he was taken to the prison in Vlasenica on about 15 May -- or 15 June 1992. He remained detained there until 13 August 1992. During the first month there, he was severely abused and beaten daily until one of the guards promised to help. After that intervention, he was not beaten at the Vlasenica prison. On 13 August 1992, the witness was taken to Batkovic camp in Bijeljina municipality. The security commander of the camp, Velibor Stojanovic, gave him the nickname Beretka 2. He was placed in a warehouse with about 1.800 prisoners. From his second day there until 11 September 1992, he was one of a group of ten prisoners who were selected out for particularly cruel treatment. They were beaten at least three times a day. On occasions, they were forced to beat one another or engage in sexual intercourse. Most often these beatings and humiliations took place in front of all the other prisoners. In late August 1992, the ICRC, Red Cross, came to Batkovic to register the prisoners. The witness's special group of ten and some of the very youngest and very oldest prisoners were taken out of the camp and hidden in the forest or nearby sheds when this visit occurred. The special group was also removed from camp when journalists came to visit. On 11 September, the witness and his nine comrades were taken to court in Bijeljina. He was ordered detained and then was taken to Doboj where he was imprisoned in a hangar or warehouse. Serb prisoners, common criminals and those who had refused to go to the front line, were allowed access to the hangar where the witness and non-Serbs were kept. These Serbs would come in any time day, night, and beat the non-Serb prisoners. Only after the prisoner manager was changed in late December 1992 did this situation change. While at Doboj, the witness and other prisoners had to engage in forced labour, sometimes digging trenches under fire at the front line. On 27 January 1993 while on detail to dig trenches at the front line, the witness was shot and wounded and hospitalised. He was eventually released as part of a prisoner exchange on 21 April 1993. The witness suffered numerous physical injuries and psychological trauma during his detention for which he has continued to receive treatment. The physical injuries included, among others, skull fracture, stab wounds, cigarette burn scars on hands and body, fracture of right arm, fractures to nose and jaw, broken ribs, damaged kidneys, and damage to the nervous system. Finally, the witness lists by name and position a number of the Serb personnel at Susica and Batkovic camps. That concludes my reading of the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kuralic, your witness statement is in evidence and will be considered by the Judges so we don't need to talk about everything that's in there but I do want to clarify a few matters with you. First of all, your municipality of Kalesija, can you tell the Court where that was located. We know for example about Zvornik municipality. Can you tell us where Kalesija was in relation to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Kalesija municipality is between Tuzla and Zvornik municipalities, somewhere halfway between or, rather, Kalesija municipality is 10 kilometres away from Tuzla and 30 kilometres away from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 7 of your statement, you talk about when refugees from Zvornik from coming to your municipality. What was the ethnicity of those refugees from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to skip ahead to paragraph 16 in your statement, Mr. Kuralic, this is after you were captured on the 30th of May, 1992, and you indicated you were taken to the command post in Memici village and you described some of the Chetniks who were there. Could you tell the Court, were they wearing any kind of uniforms and, if so, what did those uniforms look like?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms, green camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were there -- were they military or police or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: The uniforms were military. They wore military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know any of these men you saw there at the command post in Memici?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Initially, when I was captured, I didn't know anyone. When I was taken to Memici, I met Radoslav Stupar, nicknamed Raci, who used to work at the SUP in Kalesija and his brother, Slavoljub, who was my school mate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, before you were taken away from there, did you overhear any discussion about what they were going to do with you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Some of them were saying, "He ought to be used as a mine worker in Serbia." Others said that I was good for forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you were taken away from there, who took you? Was it a military person or a police person or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you were taken away from Memici to Vlasenica, who took you away, was it a military man, a policeman, or civilian?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: It was a lieutenant belonging to the unit that was positioned at Memici. They were relieved, the fresh forces were -- arrived at Memici, and that's when they took me to Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go forward then to when you were taken to Vlasenica. In paragraph 22 of your statement you talk about being taken briefly to Han Pijesak and then to Vlasenica where you saw what you describe as 350 POWs. What was the ethnicity of those 350 that you saw there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I apologise. As far as I know, these people hailed from my municipality. Most of them or perhaps all of them were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how many -- approximately how many of those 350 did you know, if they were from your municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Could the question please be repeated again? I am a bit hard of hearing on my left ear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll see if we can turn up the speaker for you. Of the 350 whom I think you said most were from your municipality --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I can't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of the 350 of whom you say many or most were from your municipality, how many of those did you know, would you say you knew, all, most, a few?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I knew most of these people. If I may correct myself, 350 to 400 people who were in that particular room mostly hailed from my municipality, that is Kalesija and the neighbouring villages, so I knew pretty well most of the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the gender of those people were, was it men, women, children, a mixture?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: A mixture of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, gender and children is mixing up age and gender and since children are only under one side of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of the spectrum, could you please explore the whole ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you give us an estimate of how many of each, how many men, how many women, and then with regard to children, if you can tell us if there was any breakdown on the children between boys and girls?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I did not have the opportunity to assess the situation in order to give you an estimate now. There were women, children, and elderly among them. But I am not able to give you the percentages because I was unable to count them and to arrive myself at a percentage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Based on that description, men, women, children, and elderly, were any of them soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Among them were those who I knew were members of the police reserve force. I also recognised among them people who were not members of any army, but there were members of Territorial Defence, members of the police reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many reserve police and TO soldiers would have been in that group?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you precisely how many there were. There might have been up to ten of those younger men there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the sports hall, who were the guards, were they civilians, military, or police?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Police. Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of those military police?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go into paragraph 27 where you talk about arriving at Susica camp where there were already 300 people in the camp where you were taken. Can you tell the Judges who those 300 people were? First of all, do you know where they were from? Did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I found out that they were from Vlasenica and the neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you find out what their ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: The ones I met, the ones I had the opportunity to talk to were Muslims and I'm not aware of whether there were any other people there of any other ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you able to find out whether they were soldiers or civilians or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, they were mostly civilians, civilians who had been taken from their homes and taken to these camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were they all men?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: No, there were women and children as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm going forward to paragraph 29 of your statement where you mention a man, Veljko Basic, who you describe as the manager for all the camps in the area. Was this the first time you'd met this person?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges how you found out about his name and his position as manager of the camps in the area?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Upon leaving this camp, I received this information from somebody from Vlasenica who knew him and who was there when I was taken and that person provided me with his name and surname afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This person had actually seen you taken away by this man; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Yes. He handcuffed me and put me in a car and drove me away to prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your statement, you say that was in Vlasenica. Do you know where that prison in Vlasenica was? Was there any building nearby that it was close to that you're aware of, any landmark you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I did not leave that prison at all, I did not go out. But according to my assessment, it was not far from the town hall, the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 30, while you were at Vlasenica prison, who were the guards there, were they civilians, police, or military?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see any Serb military or army personnel in the prison while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: You mean in the prison at Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Soldiers would come occasionally. Especially when they found out I was there in that prison, they kept coming ever more often to torture me, beat me up and generally take their frustrations out on me in different ways. And on one occasion, one person took a knife out, pointed it at me and said what eye I was using for targeting when I was shooting, and then he threatened to destroy my eye or cut off my sex organs and then one of his superiors came in and told him to go away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to put a clarifying question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm sorry, I do apologise for interrupting you but I would just like some information on -- I would like to know exactly when you talk about police, you talk to us about military police and now you're talking about police. Are you making a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. distinction between the two? How can you say that it was police and what sort of police is it? Could you perhaps reply to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. When I was taken to that prison in Vlasenica, there were guards there from MUP, from the Ministry of the Interior, so it was the civilian police and when I was at this other place, there was the military police there so that's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us is there any difference in the uniforms between the regular policemen, the civilian police and military police?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: The civilian police also had these camouflage uniforms but in blue, whereas the military police had the same uniforms in green.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to the military police in camouflage, how were you able to tell a military policeman in a green camouflage as a regular military soldier in green camouflage, was there any difference in those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: There was a difference. They had white belts and I could tell on the basis of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the Serb soldiers that you talked about coming into the gaol, do you know how they were able to get in to see you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether they were let in by the guards just like that or whether they would force their way in. I don't know. But at any rate, they would unlock the doors and come in. How they happened to come in, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know why they were seeking you out particularly?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Since on that occasion, the lieutenant or I can't remember what his rank was, but when I was arrested, he was killed and when they found out that I was there in that prison, they sought revenge and they wanted to take their wrath out on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 31, you talk about being taken from Vlasenica to Batkovic. Who were the men who took you from Vlasenica to Batkovic, were they civilians, police, military?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Military, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 33, you talk about arriving there and meeting Veljko Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would indicate in the English there is one typographical error in the fourth line at page 8, in the quote in says, "You see, you sill look even worse." It should be "You will look even worse" and I'm told that the B/C/S is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you got to Batkovic, you mentioned 1.800 people in the hangar. Again, can you tell us first of all, did you find out where these people were from?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I found out obviously that there were people there from Brezevo Polje, Brcko, Bijeljina, and of course Vlasenica, and up there around, Kalesija, Zvornik. I don't know, maybe I forgot some.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Muslim and Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the hangar where you were with the 1.800, was that all men?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were women in the other hangar as well as the elderly and the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the men that you were in the hangar with, do you know whether they were soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: What I know is that there were those four people who were members of the armed forces and I don't know about any others. They had the same treatment I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned being part of a group of ten that seemed to be selected out for special treatment. When you said there were four people who were members of the armed forces, you mean four in addition to yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I -- no, I myself plus three. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I don't know, do you have your statement in front of you? In paragraph 36, you list the other nine men that were in your special group of ten. Can you tell us which three of those were soldiers as well as you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Nedim Mustarcevic, Beretka 1; Fadil Alihodzic, Praga; and Sabin Mustafic, Vodenicar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know why you ten were chosen for this especially harsh treatment?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Us four and afterwards, the others, were added as well because initially there were not ten of news this group so after several days, other people were added to the group. But they called us Alija's fighters, as soldiers who were fighting against Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know any of these other nine men before you got to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, the --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Hannis proceeds, and I don't know whether or not I'm in a better position to see the witness than Mr. Hannis, but perhaps an inquiry might be made as to his physical comfort at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, would you like to take a break now? Are you okay to go on for a little while? Whatever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I'd like to have a short break, if possible. I need to stretch my legs a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Certainly, if that's fine with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. Mr. Hannis, could you give us an indication as far as how quickly you proceed so that we can try to make some ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have half a page here to go so 15, 20 minutes perhaps. 15 to 20 minutes, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll have a break of ten minutes now which is a short break, and after that Mr. Hannis will try to finish the examination. And then we'll have a bit of a longer break which takes approximately half an hour so ten minutes now then another perhaps 20 minutes to go, and then a longer break of half an hour. Would that suit your needs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until a quarter past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kuralic, when we broke, I was asking you about the ten of you in the special group. You mentioned that four of you were soldiers. Do you know what the other six men did or were that might have caused them to be put in this special group of Alija's fighters?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I'll start in the right order. Alija Gusalic, who was riding a horse in Bijeljina and then he threw a bomb in a Serb-owned cafe and that's why he had been declared as one of Alija's fighters. ... And then Ejub Smajic was a butcher, one of the famous people, well-known people in Bijeljina. He had a fairly good life. He was well off, but he had a considerable amount of -- considerable capital and that's why he was beaten up and that's why he was put in this group. Amer Berbic, I don't know who it was by -- on the Serb side but they said that he was gouging Serbs' eyes and that's why he was given the nickname of "the Serb cutter," and Kamberi and another one tried to run away from the camp and after a short time, they were captured again and of course they were put in this group as runaways. That's why they were called runaways. Alijaz Okanovic, they found a list of people on him. He might have been writing down the names of some people in the camp in order to, I don't know, maybe get in touch with someone else to tell them they were alive, or -- and I don't know what and he was found with that list and that's why he was placed in the same group with us and he was tortured in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to go back in your statement, you talked about the ten specials being taken out and hidden when the Red Cross came to register prisoners. Were you ten the only ones that were hidden when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: We were taken to special places, but I also found out that elderly people ages 60 and upwards and minors as well were also hidden away in other places when the Red Cross people or journalists came along.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that that happened with your group as well when journalists came to the camp. Do you know -- do you remember how many times this happened between the Red Cross visiting and journalists coming to the camp where your group was taken out and hidden?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: That month, the period of time that I spent at Batkovic, perhaps it happened some four, five, or six times I was taken out of the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, could I ask, unless you'd still have further questions on this issue of hiding prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay, then I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- if I may

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in paragraph 35 about the Serbs putting in names of Serbs to fool the Red Cross, and in your supplemental information, you expanded on that a little bit and said that Serbs actually substituted as prisoners. Can you tell the Court about that, how did you find out about that, and what were they doing exactly to hide the fact that you existed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Well, they would bring other people in to take our places, most probably those people were of Serb nationality, in order to cover up for our absence from the camp in order to make sure that there was the same number of people present. And of course another person would introduce themselves as myself, they would say that -- my name and my data, et cetera, and the Red Cross would take the data on that occasion and I would be recorded as present but I wasn't there, it was another person posing as myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know why they wouldn't want the Red Cross to see the real Mirsad Kuralic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Well, it's clear. Obviously, they had to hide me, not just myself but the other nine people who were with me in order to hide us from the public opinion because they could not show us, the state we were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Judge Orie, that was the last question I had on that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have one question. In your statement, you said, "The way they managed to get around not registering us was to put the names of some Serbs instead." Now, you explained to us that not the names of some Serbs were registered instead of your names, but that your names were registered and that they posed as if they were you. That's not exactly the same. But before we further try to understand, I'd like to ask you, how do you know exactly what they did in the paperwork?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to whether I know exactly, I don't know whether there was a mistake when it was recorded, but when we were taken out of the camp, other ten people were brought in. I don't know whether they were Serbs or who they were. I do not know. But they were brought in and these people were introduced to the Red Cross under our names, and that's how we were recorded because upon my return to the camp, I got this card, the Red Cross card. I do apologise, I don't know how this misunderstanding came about when my statement was recorded but what I've just said is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Other persons --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was not Serb names, there were people who were brought in to pose as us and they could make the numbers in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now better understand. Thank you for your information. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kuralic, I want to go next to paragraph 38 in your statement where you talked about being taken on the 11th of September to the court building in Bijeljina. Did you get any documents or paperwork in addition to the letter sending you to court? Did you get any documents or paperwork in connection with court proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I got an invitation for a hearing on the 11th of September and since, in the morning of the 11th of September, they came and called the names of all ten of us and they put us in an armoured van and they -- and then we were taken to the court building at Bijeljina and we got out of the van and were taken for this hearing, and I got a kind of written paper sentencing me to spend one month in prison until the final sentence was passed. And then I went to the court once again and we were taken to Doboj in a van.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to that paper, in paragraph 41 - I'm skipping ahead in time a bit - after you were shot and hospitalised, you mentioned that on the 1st of March you were taken back to court and the judge issued another paper. Do you still have any of those papers from your court appearances?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have nothing. I don't even have a letter of discharge from when I was in hospital. On that day, for example, when the day for the exchange of prisoners came, I was asked to relinquish all those documents and they were taken away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're talking about the 21st of April, 1993 when you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who took the papers from you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Before we set off, I was driven to the courthouse in Bijeljina, and on that occasion I was asked to relinquish all the other documents except for the International Red Cross card. But everything have having to do with the court or the hospital documents, all that was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: By whom? Who were the people that you had to give them to?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Well, a person who went with us, it was a person who also took me over as it were, and drove us to this exchange, and there was this deputy of this KP centre at Bijeljina and he took the documents from me but I don't know who he gave them to. He ordered me to empty my pockets and give him everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I want to go to paragraph 43 through 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Hanoteau would have a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've mentioned that in the beginning of September, you appeared before that tribunal. I would just like to know whether there were any judges there, prosecutor, before whom did you appear in the course of that preliminary hearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know whether the person there was a prosecutor or someone else. I appeared before the court. There was a judge there, but I wasn't familiar with the panel of judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And was it a civilian court or a military court or could you give us any indication about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that following this hearing, I was put away at the KP Dom in Bijeljina. Apparently this must have been a court of justice because that was place where criminals were sent, those who had committed criminal offences, rape, murder, and so on. So in my opinion, those were however members of the military units so that's why I believe it was a military court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was the judge hearing a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was he dressed like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you've mentioned earlier that you were in a pitiful state and one can imagine that, considering the treatment that was being dispensed to you by those wardens. Had there been no reaction in court on the part of the judge, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not sure that I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned that you were in a very bad physical state, you had received lots of blows and your physical appearance was pretty bad. And the judge before whom you appeared, didn't he look surprised or did he ask for any explanation or did he say nothing at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he didn't say anything at all. I was simply served a sentence for a one-month pre-trial detention and that's where I was to stay until the final decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this procedure was about the death of an official, or what were you being accused of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was charged with having acted in violation of the laws of Republika Srpska and waging a war against Republika Srpska; however, I'm not aware of the details that they put in the charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have another witness, Your Honour, later on who talks about the court in Bijeljina and that may address some of the questions you've raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kuralic, I want to ask you about your injuries that you talk about in paragraphs 43 through 45. Related to that, you say that you were shot on the 27th of January, 1993 and you were hospitalised at that time. But apart from that he time when you went to the hospital, between the 30th of May when you were captured and the 27th of January, 1993, after all those tortures and stabbings, cuttings and burnings and beatings, did you receive any medical treatment from your Serb captors in Vlasenica, Batkovic or Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: It was only on my arrival in Doboj the warden of the penitentiary institution there would not receive us unless we underwent a medical examination. Up until that point, I had received no medical treatments whatsoever. I had to do my best. I was left to my devices, use salt or -- I used my clothes that I would wet and then put bandages on my wounds. But even at that point that I was telling you about, I was only medically examined and I wasn't given any medical care. One could therefore say that until the 27th of January when I was taken to the hospital, I had not been given any medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you still suffering any effects, physical or psychological as a result of what happened to you during your detention?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Of course I am. I'm suffering from the consequences of what had happened to me, and every day I am faced with new medical problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand from your medical condition -- are you also suffering from PTSD, post traumatic stress disorder?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Of course I am. I suffer from lack of sleep, and then when I do fall asleep, I suffer from the nightmares taking me back to what I had gone through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to the injuries you listed in your statement, have you, since your release, been diagnosed with some kind of back problem that you relate to what happened to you during your detentions?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I think that this can be found in my documentation. On my return from the camp, I went -- I underwent a detailed medical examination and that's when I was diagnosed also with a back problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What's the nature of that problem?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Three vertebra are cracked and now I am supposed to undergo a spine operation. My left leg and arm go numb and I am supposed to operate them, I am supposed to operate my spine, my left ear was operated back in 1995, but I will have to undergo another operation. That also applies to my nose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In connection with your injuries, do you take any pain medication?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Of course I do. I have them here with me, the drugs. Do I need to show them to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that's not necessary. I want to ask you in connection with the PTSD and your medication, have you found those to ever cause you problems with your memory?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I do have difficulties remembering things; however, as far as the events at these camps are concerned, they cannot be erased from my memory. It is concerning other matters that I forget things, I tend to forget things very often. I have been doing some tests examining my head as well, and I don't know what the findings will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuralic. Those are all the questions I have for you at this time. The Defence counsel may want to ask you some questions or we may take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I suggest that we'll start cross-examination after the long break. But before we move to that, I would have one very small question, Mr. Kuralic. I find in your statement that you said that prior to the war, your village was an ethnically mixed village consisting of all nationalities with about 30 per cent of them being Serbs. Could you tell us what the approximate percentage of Muslims, Croats, others were?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I should note in relation to that, Your Honour, that was one of the corrections we made in the supplemental page when it was referring to the municipality as opposed to the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But even if it is about a municipality, yes, I did not pay sufficient care to that. I received it only this morning, of course. Could you tell us in your municipality where you said approximately 30 per cent of them being Serbs, could you tell us what the percentage of the other nationalities or ethnicities was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I used to know the exact percentages before, how many Muslims there were, how many Croats there were, how many Roma there were, how many Serbs there were. There was about 50 per cent of Muslims, then a certain percentage of Croats, a certain percentage of the Roma people, and then about 20 per cent were those categorised as "others."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, may I just ask for a clarification, you said about 30 per cent Serbs, about 50 per cent Muslims which makes 80 per cent, then you say there were Croats and Romas, and then there were some 20 per cent others, that brings us above 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I must have been misunderstood. It is under the 20 per cent that I factored Croats, Roma and others in. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's perfectly clear now and that's the most important thing. We will have a break, I would suggest, for half an hour. We'll adjourn until a quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuralic, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Loukas who is counsel for the Defence. Ms. Loukas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I can indicate that during the break I had a discussion with Mr. Hannis in relation to some medical material and it's proposed jointly that that material be placed before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is a joint conclusion by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no objection to that being presented to the Trial Chamber, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I can indicate, Your Honour, that I have the relevant B/C/S copies of the -- of the material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas, before we continue, would it not be proper that -- if it's just put to us then we have it in front of us, but if all kind of further medical details would be discussed in this courtroom, I would be a bit concerned about the privacy of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I can indicate that I propose to put these documents forward and merely to get the witness to confirm that these are his medical records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Loukas, since you are going to ask questions to the witness about them, I take it that you'd like to have them assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, yes. And I can indicate that what we have currently is the B/C/S copies so that the witness can confirm in relation to the B/C/S copies and the English copies will also be coming shortly, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The translation to arrive soon. Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Defence Exhibit D43 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kuralic, you have a copy of certain of your medical records there. Can you confirm for the Trial Chamber that they are indeed your medical records and if that takes a little bit more time to leaf through them, you may continue to do that.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that these are my medical records. If need be, I have other records here with me, for instance, the documentation relating to some medical problems that arose at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that, Mr. Kuralic, and I take it you've discussed these medical records with Mr. Hannis for the -- these further medical records with Mr. Hannis for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to the statement that's an exhibit before the Court, and that is Prosecution Exhibit P642, if that statement could be placed before you. Now, just in relation to paragraph 45 in your statement, Mr. Kuralic, you refer to ongoing treatment for psychological trauma. If you were to be asked through the Trial Chamber to produce any further records in relation to this psychological aspect, I take it they could be produced to the Court; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, also just in relation to your statement at paragraph 29 -- sorry, that's paragraph 22, you refer there to POWs, that is prisoners of war, and you gave some evidence in relation to that earlier today. Can you just indicate to the Trial Chamber what you understand by the term "prisoners of war."

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I've received an English version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph 22 we are at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. My question was -- here it is. In relation to paragraph 22, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you refer there to POWs, that is prisoners of war and you gave some evidence in relation to that earlier today. Can you just indicate to the Trial Chamber what you understand by the term "prisoner of war."

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KURALIC
utterances.text: Would you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuralic, I'll try to put the question to you. Ms. Loukas would like to know if the statement says prisoners of war, what are prisoners of war in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, one can distinguish between prisoners of war who were members of a military and civilian victims that were taken prisoner. Generally speaking, all of these are prisoners of war regardless of whether they were captured in their homes or elsewhere because the entire territory was affected by war and that's why I merely found it more -- I found it easier to use the term "prisoners of war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I then understand that you consider prisoners of war all those who were taken prisoner during and -- the war and in the territory where the war took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuralic, I first have to ask Mr. Hannis whether there are any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuralic, you are aware that your written statement is in evidence so the fact that you've testified in this court for approximately one hour does not mean that that's all the information you've given to us because we have your statement and we'll look carefully to its content as well. You further have answered questions by the Prosecution, you've answered a few questions by the Defence, and a few questions put to you by the Bench. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague because this Chamber is aware that because of your state of health, that it might not have been easy for you and you also testified that not only your physical health is affected by the events now more than 10 years ago, as you described them, but also that you're still suffering psychologically from it. Therefore, we'd like to thank you thoroughly for coming to The Hague and we wish you first of all, to the extent possible, that your treatment will improve your health and that you will have a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for having invited me to testify before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Kuralic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I did understand that Mr. Margetts will take the next witness; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I was waiting to hear from the Bench whether you wanted us to resume immediately with the next witness or if we could start with him tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we start with the exhibits -- no, I think we dealt with all the exhibits, Madam Registrar, because there were only very limited number, so we have dealt already with the -- apart from that, we have not yet heard from the Defence whether there were any objections. They have just been assigned numbers and the same is true for D43 which has been assigned a number, but I do understand at least that for D43, there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and there's no objection to the Prosecution Exhibits. Just in relation to the scheduling, of course, if I might interpose in relation to that question at this point, Mr. Hannis of course, inquired this morning in relation to a request by Mr. Margetts to commence the evidence in chief tomorrow. I can indicate that I have no opposition to that in view of the fact that there is only the two witnesses scheduled this week and on my part, I'd also like to put in a request, I'm not entirely certain as to how long the evidence in chief would take, but Your Honour, if it might proceed by way of evidence in chief in relation to the next witness or Tuesday, and my cross-examination on the Wednesday, Your Honour. I can indicate in relation to one of the documents in particular, the translation is not complete. As I understand and it's a fairly significant document. That's one aspect, but in terms of the sort of scheduling in terms of the -- both the Prosecution and the Defence dealing with this week, it would be of great assistance to be able to deal with the next witness in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine. On the other hand, there is still a lot of work to be done also by the Judges apart from this case, and therefore, of course, in looking at all the messages we received, at least the Judges were scheduling more extensive meetings for Thursday morning and we'd not very much would like to give that up. I mean if there is any chance that the next witness would not be finished by next Wednesday, both chief and cross --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There's no question, Your Honour -- sorry, if I might interpose at that point. If it were to be broken up in that way, the Tuesday and the Wednesday, I could guarantee that Your Honour that we would have no problem about going into Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the problem. We want to start now, so that we have Thursday available for other matters unless the parties could guarantee that we would finish by Wednesday and then of course we could delay the start of the next witness. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I had asked Mr. Margetts for his estimate on time in direct, he indicated to me it was between 3 and 5 hours, depending partly on what resolution he and Ms. Loukas were able to reach using the 89(F) procedure, and I'm not sure what status that is. What I understand Ms. Loukas to say is that she believes if we started direct tomorrow and Mr. Margetts finished all his direct by the end of the day tomorrow, that we would be done with that witness by the end of the day on Wednesday. Perhaps I could call and ask Mr. Margetts, he's on extension ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean the Chamber would be willing to take the risk because there are some procedural matters pending as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts is on his way. Perhaps I better wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting, may I ask another question regarding a prior witness, Mr. Bjelobrk. There was an outstanding question on whether he would be required to return. I don't know if Your Honours have had a chance to reach a final decision on that matter, but we're trying to figure out whether we need to try and schedule him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- I can tell you it's constantly on our mind. It's one of the procedural issues we'd like to deal with. We'd like to find time for this week perhaps we could provide the parties with a list of what to expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. We are discussing at this moment the scheduling for this week. We could start with the next witness now, although I do understand that you'd prefer to start tomorrow; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We would prefer to start tomorrow. There is a small amount of material that we'd like to show to the witness this afternoon, it's not absolutely essential that we show that material to him this afternoon before commencing. The outstanding issue is whether or not it will be substantially 89(F) or alternatively most of the evidence will be viva voce, and we need to resolve that with the Defence. If we were to start, I think we'd need probably an hour to resolve that issue and prepare the appropriate material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also did understand that your estimate on how much time you'd need was anything between two and five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, Your Honour, I can indicate that as I've indicated previously, and I've already communicated this to Mr. Margetts, I certainly have no objection to Mr. Margetts commencing tomorrow and my further application is that I commence on the -- the Wednesday. In relation, of course, to the issue of the usage of 89(F) and the extent of the usage, obviously that's a question that I would need some time to sit down with Mr. Margetts and sort through -- and it is rather voluminous material, I should indicate, Your Honour, that we both need to go through and specifically clarify what can proceed under 89(F) and to what the Defence would have an objection to proceeding by way of 89(F). So there is those clarifying matters to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. If Mr. Margetts were to start tomorrow, and if you would need nevertheless five hours, then he would not finish by tomorrow because we only have four effective hours a day. That would bring us quite well into next Wednesday. Therefore, it's still to be seen whether the cross-examination could be concluded on that same Wednesday and we also still have a we have a number of procedural issues to deal with. If today we would have another -- well, let's say, one and a half hours, close to two hours, tomorrow would have four hours, the day after tomorrow would have four hours, that makes a total of nine and a half. If, by the manoeuvreing of the parties, we finally would end up in a situation where we would have to sit on Thursday, where the examination-in-chief at its maximum is assessed at -- estimated at 5 hours, then we would then we would cut the hearings in small bits and pieces which the Chamber is not quite happy with since we want to know if only two witnesses then we have, in our view, at least, nine and a half hours from now on, we would have our Thursday available to schedule other matters. Therefore, if we would not start at this moment, I would like to have a clear commitment of the parties on what the scheduling would look like, whether we would finish by Wednesday; if not, the Chamber would prefer to start right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As an immediate solution, what we also could do is to have a break now for one hour and see if the parties could come to such an agreement on how to proceed that we'll finish by Wednesday. We'd then start tomorrow. If you do not agree then after one hour from now on or after 45 minutes, we just restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think that speaking from the Prosecution's point of view, we could resume in 45 minutes and we'd be able to give that indication then.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, well, two matters. Your Honour asked firstly for a clear commitment from the Defence perspective, I think we're in a position to give that clear commitment firstly, but secondly, the approach that Your Honour suggests in relation to Mr. Margetts and I spending the next 45 minutes trying to sort out what can and cannot be dealt with in 89(F) may be productive and I'm happy to undertake that course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So let's then -- we'll then now adjourn until 12.30, then we'll hear from the parties whether there is a joint proposal for the next witness concluding not later than Wednesday, preferably one hour before the Wednesday hearing ends so that we would have some time for procedural matters so we could not have to reconvene on Thursday just for the procedural matters. So we'll hear from your proposals. If there's no proposal which would meet the requirements of the Chamber then we would start at 12.30 with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If Your Honour please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it the Prosecution or the Defence that will take the floor first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, since our submissions are likely to be the same, I'm willing to take the floor. We've reached substantial agreement in respect of the 89(F) material and it's expected that the Prosecution will be able to complete its examination-in-chief by the second break tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Ms. Loukas, 89(F) sometimes asks for more time for cross-examination than the 60 per cent guidance.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that -- in this case, how much time do you expect it will take you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: As Mr. Margetts indicated, our discussions were fruitful and we were able to come to some considerable agreement in relation to certain matters and a substantial agreement in relation to 89(F). On this question of an assessment of time, it's my assessment, Your Honour, that if Mr. Margetts finishes within the first two sessions tomorrow, I would come well within the first two sessions on Wednesday -- and leaving sufficient time for the housekeeping matters. There's one matter that I would raise in relation to a specific portion of the statement, there's a matter to which I object to in its entirety and, Your Honour, that's a matter that obviously would have to be argued before Your Honours. In those circumstances, I'm happy to make that argument now or leave that for tomorrow morning but I wanted to place before Your Honours that there was this question of a specific portion that I objected to in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, any problem to have this dealt with at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Ms. Loukas, you may proceed. I'm just trying to find the material for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will wait until Your Honour has the statement before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, in relation -- Your Honours, in relation to the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the statement of the 24th, 25th of April, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's the statement of the 24th of April, 2003, and the 25th of April, 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, if Your Honour turn to page 2 of the statement and carrying over to the top of page 3, there's -- what's contained in the statement is from this particular witness in relation to what his perception of the role of the speaker of the Assembly was, that's contained in the last paragraph of page 2 and continues there. Additionally, if one goes to the following paragraph, the first full paragraph on the top of page 3, there's this question of the highest ranking or what have you, toward the middle of the paragraph there. Now, Your Honour, just in relation to -- and more specifically in relation to those matters contained in the bottom paragraph of page 2 and the top paragraph of page 3, I would object to opinion evidence coming from this witness in relation to the position of Mr. Krajisnik and his roles and responsibilities as speaker of the Assembly. It's quite clear from the statement that the discussions that this witness had with Mr. Krajisnik in relation to the construction of a road, Your Honour, this witness is not in the position of being some sort of expert on the role and responsibilities of the speaker of the parliament or the president of the Assembly and, Your Honour, this sort of evidence, Your Honour, does not come into a category that would be of assistance to the Trial Chamber. The sort of evidence in relation to the roles and responsibility and the hierarchy in relation to those roles and responsibilities is, of course, evidence that may come from an expert witness in relation to the political structure and what have you, firstly; and secondly, factual witnesses who actually have an insight into the inside workings, as it were, of the processes. So in my submission, Your Honours, evidence from somebody discussing a -- a road construction project and then a group of dignitaries attending, as it were, a function of the construction of a tunnel and, bearing in mind the political relation of the situation, I would submit that that's not the sort of evidence that's going to assist the Trial Chamber in assessing the questions that are very much in the forefront the Trial Chamber's considerations. And in view of the fact that this is witness that cannot give expert evidence in relation to this very important question and cannot give the necessary sort of factual detail in relation to the questions that are being considered by the Trial Chamber, but rather gives impressionistic opinions and the generalised view of a -- of a layperson on the questions and not somebody with any particular insight into the processes that Your Honours need evidence upon. To give evidence of this general, speculative, impressionistic nature, Your Honour, is evidence that the Defence would object to most strenuously and we seek its deletion and seek that it not be introduced by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't present this witness as a witness in the first category that Ms. Loukas referred to, that being an expert in political matters. What we present him as is a factual witness who does have an insight into the inside working of the governmental processes and that's the second category that Ms. Loukas acknowledged would be a relevant -- in that second category, witnesses of that nature would be able to give relevant evidence. Why we say that is the following: He was a member of the communist party from 1968. From 1991, he was a member of the SDP. Between 1986 and 1992, he was the general manager of the public construction company for railway tracks from Tuzla to Zvornik which, I don't know relatively what scale that project was, but it was certainly one of the major projects that was ongoing in Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war and he was the general manager of that project. He's also someone that took a leading -- that had a leading role in the Zvornik community.
