He states -- in the statement it refers to the fact that this project that he was managing required him to regularly report to the Prime Minister Jure Pelivan and the minister of finance so in that role which we can only see the details of it from the statement here, he was intimately involved at a very high level in the workings of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian state, and in that capacity, he had occasion to invite dignitaries and participate with dignitaries in early 1991 in the meeting that is described in his statement. Effectively he was responsible for inviting people because he understood who it was that were the decision makers in the Bosnia and Herzegovinian state. It won't be the first time that the Court has heard evidence of nature to which the way in which the state was organised and in fact the way in which the state has functioned. This witness is able to give the Court factual information as to how, in fact, the accused exercised his role in the Bosnia and Herzegovinian parliament during a period which is relevant for our indictment and substantial matters were attended to, substantial events took place at the time that the accused was the speaker of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian parliament and this witness is able to indicate to the Court the power that was in the hands of the accused at that time. And on that basis, we say this is relevant evidence and this is a matter that we should be able to proceed on tomorrow. We say what weight that the Court will assign this evidence ultimately will depend obviously on many different factors that we need not go into. One of which, of course, will be whether or not this evidence is corroborated by other witnesses that have come before the Court, and we say it is. And we say it's the exercise of power by the accused during this period is a critical issue for the Court and accordingly, we apply to ask questions about this topic viva voce tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might brief respond to the points made by Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may briefly do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Firstly, the basis that Mr. Margetts puts forward for the admission of this sort of evidence is that -- well, he began with the witness was a member of the communist party. I don't think that in any way assists the Trial Chamber. The second point was that he was the general manager of a public construction company. Again, I don't know that that, in any way, assists the Trial Chamber in making the determination that I've sought from Your Honours. Mr. Margetts also raises the point that this particular witness was reporting to the then-Prime Minister and also to the Minister for Finance and, importantly, certainly not reporting to Mr. Krajisnik, that's clear from his statement. Additionally, Mr. Margetts makes the point that the witness was in a position of inviting dignitaries on the basis of their being decision makers in the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Being in a position to invite dignitaries in relation to what's perceived to be potential decision makers is simply not enough for the Trial Chamber to receive this as probative evidence in relation to questions that are before the Trial Chamber. Then Mr. Margetts goes on to indicate that the -- this witness would be able to produce factual information as to the role played by the president of the Assembly but this witness can give Your Honours no more than what Your Honours are already aware of: Mr. Krajisnik was the president of the Assembly. In addition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you follow the approach taken by Mr. Margetts that you are at this moment, you are very much expressing yourself on the weight to be given to the evidence. As far as the admissibility issue is concerned, I understood you well that Mr. Margetts, before he entered into a lot of details, said that this was a witness who could testify about relevant facts and your position was that he was a witness that could give us irrelevant opinions which you either characterised as impressionistic, I mean that's the issue. And now to say if you really have in mind that this Chamber would consider the fact that someone is a general manager of construction companies who invites dignitaries being as such relevant for hearing his testimony, I would have at least some 500 candidates who all -- of course it should all be seen in the context and what you both started doing is to create the context and to tell the Court that the weight to be given to all these facts was such that we should admit the matters -- the -- this statement in evidence. I think you're mixing up the admissibility test and what to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect, the point that I seek to make in relation to evidence of this nature is that I think Your Honour quite rightly characterises the fact that there are questions to be determined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you tell us that the could bring us nothing more than Mr. Krajisnik was the speaker of the Assembly. Of course that's still to be seen. It's not -- it's not that, I would say, simplistic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might just briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Briefly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Add to that point that Your Honour has made. The point is this: Whilst this can be categorised as merely a discussion on the question of weight. It is more than that, because my submissions, Your Honour, are directed to the fact that there is no weight that Your Honours could possibly bring to these matters that are contained within the statement. It is on that basis that I ask Your Honours to not allow this evidence. Whilst it could be categorised as merely a discussion about weight, when one considers the factors to be considered, Your Honours, my submission is you would not allow this into evidence because there is no weight that can be attached to the evidence sought to be put forward by the Prosecution through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, and that would start exactly where, where the weight is missing, is that starting with "My perception of the role of the speaker."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would go until where, exactly so we know where, upon what part to concentrate.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well it goes from "My perception ..." until "President of the Presidency, the speaker, and the Prime Minister." Then that sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see where -- you're still -- "It is my perception that," then three lines later you say it's the speaker and the Prime Minister. That's where it stops. Then it gains a bit of weight again after that or "my discussion with Krajisnik was strictly business related and involved," seems rather factual.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no problem with factual evidence, it's this opinion-based evidence that I object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's just the first four lines or is there another portion? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll just check the next paragraph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, and just in relation to that, there is there's just a sentence in the middle of the very next paragraph, "Momcilo Krajisnik was the highest ranked of our visitors." Again, that's this ranking concept is in my view purely, at this point, baseless opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Impressionistic --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But the main -- impressionistic and what have you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That was the other line, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's basically those lines that I've identified on page 2 and the line I've identified on page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Margetts, I hardly can imagine that you would still like to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just looking for the line on page 3, "Momcilo Krajisnik was the highest ranking" ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not going to discuss now whether someone could be -- the Chamber will of course look at whether a civilian is in a position to say who is a high-ranking, a higher-ranking, the highest-ranking, the top-ranking, the upper-top-ranking, and then finally also the Chamber will consider whether it makes that much difference on whether you say high or higher or highest and what conclusions could be drawn from that. Is there any other matter at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That is basically the portion of the statement that I object to and I have made my arguments clear in relation to what I consider to be the lack of weight of that particular evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're starting to repeat it again. Yes, you made yourself clear. Then the parties should keep themselves available tomorrow if we might have a few decisions to be delivered. If you are finishing before the second break we might use that time then that would certainly not be more than five up to 12 or 13 minutes to deliver one or more decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00 same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be reconvened on Tuesday, the 26th day of April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
